opportunities.title: Microbiome for terrestrial livestock sustainability and health within a One Health approach
opportunities.description:
Expected Outcome: Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes: the research community, farmers, livestock industry e.g. breeders, service providers, policymakers understand better the role of the microbiome on livestock health and production and the interaction with environment and human health within a One Health approach; researchers' communities and innovators in the livestock sector have access to a platform of tools for data sharing, knowledge exchange, capacity building and standardization in microbiome research and its applications through synergies with other platforms in a One Health context; targeted strategies and guidelines are available to farmers, service providers and livestock industry to contribute to improving livestock health, while reducing antimicrobial use and environmental impact, and securing animal welfare. Scope: Microbiome research offers transformative potential for livestock management within the One Health (OH) framework, which emphasises the interconnected health of animals, humans, and the environment. In livestock, microbiome innovation can address pressing issues such as antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and zoonotic disease transmission. However, gaps persist in understanding the role of variability within host-microbiome interactions, in developing sustainable farming practices, and assessing these interventions in real-world farming settings. Advancing microbiome research can enhance animal health and productivity, improve ecosystems, while reducing environmental and climate impacts. By focusing on microbiome-based solutions, the objective is to support sustainable livestock systems that align with OH principles, necessitating cross-disciplinary collaboration to ensure comprehensive health benefits. Proposals should address all of the following activities: investigate the microbiome of terrestrial livestock, their influence on animal health, taking into account the holobiont/hologenome perspectives, and the interactions with the environment (soil, plant, water, air) and human health; develop integrated data monitoring systems that track microbiome related health indicators across livestock, plant, and human health sectors, and help in risk assessment models for zoonotic disease and/or AMR emergence and transmission; assess how microbiome-based solutions for animal health affect, and are affected by, soil and plant health, and the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides; design holistic health models that incorporate microbiome research to enhance the robustness of animals as well as animal health and welfare, and overall productivity, taking into account soil and plant health, and to assess potential synergies and trade-offs between these objectives; design microbiome related intervention strategies to prevent outbreaks and cross-species transmission in animal populations and reduce the risk of zoonosis, thereby contributing to reduced antimicrobial usage while enhancing resilience, animal welfare, and minimizing environmental impact; develop, or contribute to, platforms to collaboratively assess and optimise the efficacy and implementation of microbiome-based tools, products and services in the livestock sector through synergies with other platforms within a One Health context; enhance collaboration among veterinarians, microbiologists, geneticists, animal and plant biologists, epidemiologists, and ecologists and other experts to work towards a One Health approach. Projects selected under this topic should interact between themselves and build on/interact with recent or on-going EU funded projects and initiatives, including those funded under the topic HORIZON-CL6-2026-02-FARM2FORK-11: Integrating a holistic perspective in microbiome research for resilient, competitive and sustainable food systems, as well as with relevant activities of the European partnerships on animal health and welfare, on One health AMR, and on pandemic preparedness. The projects under this topic are relevant to the EU policies related to the EU Green Deal’s goals for resilient and sustainable agri-food systems, the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Life Sciences strategy, the Vision for Agriculture and Food, the EU One Health Action Plan against Antimicrobial Resistance, and the Council Recommendation on stepping up EU actions to combat antimicrobial resistance in a One Health approach.

Erwartetes Ergebnis: Von den Projektergebnissen wird erwartet, dass sie zu allen folgenden erwarteten Ergebnissen beitragen: transdisziplinäre Forschungsgemeinschaften arbeiten zusammen, um die Gesundheit von Ökosystemen und wildlebenden Arten (einschließlich Physiologie, genetischer Vielfalt, Bevölkerungsverteilung und Ökologie) angesichts der bestehenden und aufkommenden Stressfaktoren, die durch die indirekten und direkten Ursachen des Verlusts an biologischer Vielfalt (einschließlich, aber nicht beschränkt auf Klimawandel und Umweltverschmutzung) verursacht werden, durch verstärktes Wissen und Monitoring vorherzusagen; politische Entscheidungsträger, Behörden, Interessenträger und Bürgerinnen und Bürger die Zusammenhänge zwischen der Gesundheit wildlebender Arten und Ökosysteme, der Gesundheit von Haustieren und Pflanzen sowie der menschlichen Gesundheit besser verstehen. Die Fortschritte von Behörden und politischen Entscheidungsträgern auf dem Weg zu einer umfassenden Governance im Rahmen des Konzepts „Eine Gesundheit“ werden dank der Entwicklung wissenschaftlich fundierter Indikatoren bewertet. Anwendungsbereich: Der Ansatz „Eine Gesundheit“ erkennt den inhärenten Zusammenhang zwischen der Gesundheit von Ökosystemen, Wildtieren, Menschen, Haustieren und Pflanzen an. Dieser Ansatz ist von entscheidender Bedeutung, um Gesundheitsbedrohungen sektorübergreifend zu verhindern, zu antizipieren, zu erkennen und darauf zu reagieren. Sie hat das Potenzial, die Auswirkungen und gesellschaftlichen und wirtschaftlichen Kosten solcher Bedrohungen zu verringern und ihr Entstehen zu verhindern und gleichzeitig die Belastung der Umwelt zu verringern, zur Ernährungssicherheit beizutragen und den Zugang zu sauberer Luft und sauberem Wasser sicherzustellen. Die Vorschläge sollten die Ziele und die Umsetzung des Grünen Deals der EU, der EU-Biodiversitätsstrategie für 2030 und des Globalen Biodiversitätsrahmens von Kunming-Montreal sowie des Globalen Aktionsplans für Biodiversität und Gesundheit des Übereinkommens über die biologische Vielfalt (CBD) [1] unterstützen. opportunities.description:

Anwendungsbereich: Invasive gebietsfremde Arten sind eine der fünf Hauptursachen für den Verlust der biologischen Vielfalt. Abgesehen davon, dass viele invasive gebietsfremde Arten der Natur und der Wirtschaft großen Schaden zufügen, erleichtern sie auch den Ausbruch und die Ausbreitung von Infektionskrankheiten und stellen eine Bedrohung für Menschen und einheimische Wildtiere dar. Die Zahl der Neuansiedlungen invasiver gebietsfremder Arten hat in den letzten Jahren zugenommen. Ohne wirksame Kontrollmaßnahmen werden die Risiken für unsere Natur und Gesundheit weiter steigen. Klimawandel und Landnutzungsänderungen erleichtern die Verbreitung und Etablierung vieler gebietsfremder Arten. Es wird erwartet, dass die Vorschläge die Prävention, Tilgung und/oder Bewirtschaftung invasiver gebietsfremder Arten durch die Interessenträger unterstützen, einschließlich adaptiver Bewirtschaftungsansätze. Dieses Thema steht im Zusammenhang mit Ziel 12 der EU-Biodiversitätsstrategie für 2030 (Verringerung der Zahl der von invasiven gebietsfremden Arten bedrohten Arten auf der Roten Liste um 50 %) und Ziel 6 des Globalen Biodiversitätsrahmens von Kunming-Montreal: Verringerung der Einführung invasiver gebietsfremder Arten um 50 % bis 2030 und Minimierung ihrer Auswirkungen. Die Vorschläge sollten die Umsetzung der EU-Verordnung über die Wiederherstellung der Natur, der EU-Verordnung über invasive gebietsfremde Arten und der Meeresstrategie-Rahmenrichtlinie unterstützen. Die Vorschläge sollten darauf abzielen, einige Wissenslücken zu schließen, die bei der IPBES-Bewertung invasiver gebietsfremder Arten (2023) [1] festgestellt wurden. Alle Arten von Ökosystemen (terrestrische, frische und/oder marine Gewässer) können behandelt werden. Erfolgreiche Vorschläge sollten: Einrichtung von mindestens drei Living Labs mit jeweils 10 bis 20 Versuchsstandorten nach den drei wichtigsten Grundsätzen: a) gemeinsame Gestaltung mit einer Vielzahl von Interessenträgern, b) in realen Umgebungen und c) unter Einbeziehung der Endnutzer. Grenzüberschreitende Living Labs werden gefördert, und Living Labs werden voraussichtlich in mindestens drei verschiedenen EU-Mitgliedstaaten und/oder assoziierten Ländern angesiedelt sein. opportunities.description: Autoimmune in Menopause and Pregnancy Transitions NEW $50M PROGRAM Jointly funded by Pivotal Apply Now ABSTRACT PORTAL OPEN 25 NOVEMBER 2026 AT 11:59PM ET. Download the full program announcement here . Women represent 4 out of 5 autoimmune disease patients, more than 400 million women globally. 1,2 Autoimmune disease costs each affected woman 4 to 9 healthy, productive years over a lifetime, the equivalent of losing 1 or more days every week to pain, fatigue, and joint swelling. 3 Despite this disproportionate impact, no existing therapy addresses a woman’s unique risk or its biological causes. What accounts for the disproportionate risk women experience, and what can be done to reduce it? Why women? A woman’s risk for autoimmune disease is not fixed; risk rises and falls with her hormone transitions, surging at puberty, after childbirth, and around menopause. In the 3 months after the birth of her first child, a woman’s risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis (RA) rises about 5-fold. 4 If she reaches menopause before 45, her risk of seronegative RA more than doubles. 5 Multiple sclerosis (MS) quiets in the third trimester of pregnancy, then relapses rise 6-fold postpartum. 6 Across the menopausal transition, markers of nerve-cell injury rise and neurologic function declines, 7 and disability progression is nearly twice as common after menopause. 8 Lupus tracks hormone transitions differently. Flares are nearly twice as common in pregnancy, 9 activity rises in the late postpartum months, 10 and again in the final year of perimenopause. 11 The timing is not a coincidence. The timing is the signal. Estrogen dynamically regulates self-tolerance , the immune system’s ability to distinguish the body’s own tissues from foreign threats, and as estrogen rises and falls across a woman’s life, self-tolerance shifts with it. 12–14 Yet autoimmune disease models fail to incorporate immune–endocrine state, or to distinguish true hormonal state from chronological aging, and no therapy is guided by a woman’s immune–endocrine transitions. Estrogen is a rheostat for the immune system Immune cells carry estrogen receptors, and through them estrogen tunes how strongly the immune system reacts while preserving self-tolerance. 15,16 Estrogen acts on 2 dials. Central tolerance , operating in the thymus, screens out self-reactive T cells before they enter the bloodstream. Rising estrogen lowers the efficiency of this screening by downregulating the thymic protein AIRE. 14 Peripheral tolerance , the backup, is enforced by regulatory T cells (Tregs) . Estrogen expands Tregs and strengthens their immune-suppressive capacity. 13,17,18 Tregs rise in pregnancy, deepening immune tolerance to the developing fetus; after delivery, when MS and RA flares cluster, Tregs decline. 19 At menopause, estrogen’s lasting decline impairs Treg function 20 and tips the balance toward inflammation. 21 One lever, different effects. The direction estrogen tips the immune system depends on its level, the local tissue context, and timing. In RA and MS, disease tends to quiet under the high estrogen of pregnancy and flare when estrogen withdraws after delivery, a pattern that points to peripheral tolerance. Lupus runs the opposite way, worsening when estrogen is high. In lupus the dominant players are self-reactive B cells , the immune cells that generate autoantibodies directed at the body’s own DNA, proteins, and cells, which drive inflammation . Estrogen promotes self-reactive B cell survival and autoantibody output, so the same high-estrogen state that calms RA and MS inflames lupus. One hormone, acting through different immune routes, protects in some diseases and provokes in others. These 3 diseases, spanning opposite ends of that spectrum, are the program’s index cases. A high burden at pivotal chapters RA, MS, and lupus affect nearly 20 million women globally, who together forfeit more than 6 million healthy life-years each year. All 3 diseases are growing, with RA alone projected to affect more than 30 million people by 2050. 22 After onset, RA costs a woman about 1.8 days a week, MS 2.5, and lupus 3.3. Those lost days fall disproportionately at 2 chapters. The first chapter is the year after childbirth. More than 500,000 women a year face their sharpest rise in disease activity postpartum: more than a quarter of women with MS relapse within 3 months, 6 and close to 2 in 5 women with RA flare. 23 For others the postpartum period brings disease onset, with RA risk roughly 5 times higher than at other times 4 , with an estimated 30,000 new RA cases a year traced to this window alone. The second chapter is the menopausal transition. opportunities.description: Breadcrumb Home Our Work Research Grants and Awards Share Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin More Places to Share Basil O’Connor Starter Scholar Research Awards Save to Dashboard Saved Pages Supporting outstanding researchers who are embarking on or continuing their independent research careers. Named in honor of the first March of Dimes Chairman and President, the Basil O'Connor Starter Scholar Research Award is comprised of a $150,000 grant over a two-year period. It prioritizes investigators proposing to conduct impactful research studies that will advance our translational understanding of, or lead to improved clinical treatment of, serious medical conditions that affect the health of a woman’s pregnancy or the health of moms and newborns in the first year postpartum. Recipients are conducting concerted translational research in line with their personal and professional interests that will one day grow into a body of distinguished work that sheds light on the U.S. maternal and infant health crisis. Reflective of our mission, applications should focus on preterm birth and health equity. They should clearly outline a path from discovery to functional studies to clinical translation, with the eventual goal to cure or greatly mitigate conditions that adversely impact the health of pregnant women and newborns. Award amount: $150,000 over two years Areas of research: Serious medical conditions that affect the health of a woman’s pregnancy and/or moms and newborns within the first year postpartum. Open to: Applicants, who at award date, are four to nine years past the last year of, in the case of MD or MD/PhD, clinical training required for medical specialty board certification or, in the case of PhD scientists, completion of their terminal degree. MD/PhD applicants must hold a full-time tenure-track faculty position (or equivalent) at their current U. S. based institution. PhD applicants must have either primary or secondary appointments in clinical departments related to maternal or child health. Those who have previously received a Basil O’Connor Award are not eligible. Note: The current cycle is closed Application portal opens: February 27, 2026 Application portal closes: May 29, 2026 Notification of awards: Planned mid-September 2026 Award start date: October 1, 2026 Award end date: September 30, 2028 Apply on portal Eligibility The Basil O’Connor Starter Scholar Research Award is intended to be an early-career grant to investigators who are embarking on an independent research career. Eligibility is thus restricted. Please consider: At award date, MD or MD/PhD applicants should be four to nine years past the last year of clinical training required for medical specialty board certification and must hold a full-time tenure-track faculty position (or equivalent) at their current U.S. based institution. At award date, PhD scientists should be four to nine years past completion of their terminal degree. They must have either primary or secondary appointments in clinical departments related to maternal or child health. Applicants who have transition faculty-mentored awards (e.g. K99/R00) are welcome if they still have one year of the mentored portion. If not, application should be deferred. K12 and K08 grantees are encouraged to apply. Candidates may not simultaneously hold a grant for any other March of Dimes research program. Applicants may not have total grant support exceeding $200,000 per year before the Basil O'Connor Award start date (e.g. R01). Those who have previously received a Basil O’Connor Award are not eligible. Requests for exceptions to the four-to-nine-year eligibility window (e.g., extensions due to parental leave or other qualifying circumstances) may be submitted to the Research Grants Department at [email protected] . How to apply The entire application must be completed online at https://modresearchgrants.aibs-scores.org . Each application should be accompanied by a letter of nomination from the applicant’s chair; please see below for more details. Included in the letter of nomination should be: Nominator’s name, academic appointment, mailing address, telephone number, and email address. opportunities.title: Reproductive Scientist Development Program
opportunities.description: Breadcrumb Home Our Work Research Grants and Awards Share Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin More Places to Share Reproductive Scientist Development Program No matter where in their early-career path applicants find themselves, scholars must be committed to a career in OB-GYN and medical research, ready to use the Reproductive Scientist Development Program as a springboard into the type of deeper and more targeted scientific inquiry their careers will ask of them. Save to Dashboard Saved Pages The Reproductive Scientist Development Program is more flexible in terms of research proposals Due to its focus on early stage scientists who may not have had rigorous experience or training in scientific inquiry or publication, recipient acceptance into the program does not imply a need to conduct and publish novel, breakthrough scientific work in the OB-GYN space, as this in and of itself is rare. Rather, the program is a March of Dimes effort to recognize and strengthen the wide breadth of talent in the OB-GYN field and spark a lifelong confidence, passion, and commitment to maternal fetal health research that will change both clinical outcomes and lives in the decades to come. As such, research proposals must be translational in nature and relate to the field of maternal fetal health — with a focus on prematurity, maternal and infant morbidity and mortality, and health equity. While the outcome of the work is important, we know that the training and shaping of the recipient during the grant period is what will lead to better and more impactful work in the future. This program is administrated by a host institution and is funded by a coalition of organizations including March of Dimes. Each coalition member pools funding to support the research work of about a dozen grant recipients annually. Recent changed in the grant structure now allows a coalition organization to fund a specific recipient. Award amount: $250,000 over two years in salary support Areas of research: Obstetrics and gynecology and their subspecialties (e.g., reproductive endocrinology and infertility) Open to: An MD/DO degree and OB-GYN residents near completion of residency or near completion of subspecialty fellowship For program year 2027: Letter of intent deadline: May 15, 2026 Application deadline: July 1, 2026 at 5 p.m. ET Notification of acceptance: No later than November 15, 2026 This grant is managed by the host institution of the Reproductive Scientist Development Program Learn how to apply Eligibility Must be seeking a career in academic obstetrics and gynecology research. Applicants must be near completion of their residency in obstetrics and gynecology or in their subspecialty fellowship. Any individual with the skills, knowledge, and resources necessary to carry out the proposed research is invited to work with their institution to develop an application for support. Individuals from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups as well as individuals with disabilities are always encouraged to apply. Potential applicants should promptly contact the Reproductive Scientist Development Program office, as should the sponsoring Department Chair. MD or DO degree. U.S. citizen, noncitizen national, or been lawfully admitted for permanent residence and possess an Alien Registration Receipt Card (I-151or I 155) or some other verification of legal admission as a permanent citizen at the time of the award. Completion of a four-year internship and residency in obstetrics-gynecology approved by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada by the time the Reproductive Scientist Development Program training would begin. Prior laboratory experience is not a requirement for applicants, although a research proposal is required as part of the application. How to apply Note: This application process is managed by the host insitition of the Reproductive Scientist Development Program. March of Dimes does not manage this application process. Before submitting this application, the Reproductive Scientist Development Program requires that the applicant submit a letter of intent to the Reproductive Scientist Development Program office indicating: name of department of OB-GYN sponsor, name and address of proposed scientific mentor, and brief description of the proposed research project. This will be reviewed by the Program Director and feedback will be provided to potential applicants. The Reproductive Scientist Development Program advises that applicants contact the Reproductive Scientist Development Program office by phone or email to confirm eligibility requirements prior to submission of a letter of intent or an application. Application deadlines to begin program for July 2026: Receipt of letter of intent: May 15, 2026 Receipt of Application: July 1, 2026 by 5 p.m. ET Selection: Interviews of candidates by the Selection Committee will take place in August/September at a time

Rather, the program is a March of Dimes effort to recognize and strengthen the wide breadth of talent in the pediatrics field and spark a lifelong confidence, passion, and commitment to fetal, neonatal, and childhood health research that will change both clinical outcomes and lives in the decades to come. Award amount: $250,000 over two years Areas of research: Pediatrics and its subspecialties Open to: An MD, MD/PhD, or DO degree and pediatric residents near completion/completion of residency or first year of subspecialty fellowship For program year 2027: Letter of intent deadline: February 16, 2026 Application deadline: April 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: No later than December 31, 2026 This grant is managed by the host institution of the Pediatric Scientist Development Program Learn how to apply Eligibility Candidates must be completing or have completed pediatric residency in the U.S.A. or Canada. Please note that a maximum of 25% of training positions are available for MD/PhD applicants each year. Candidates with PhD degrees alone are not eligible. opportunities.title: Agnes Higgins Award in Maternal-Fetal Nutrition
opportunities.description: Breadcrumb Home Our Work Research Grants and Awards Share Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin More Places to Share Agnes Higgins Award in Maternal-Fetal Nutrition The Agnes Higgins Award recognizes distinguished achievement in research, education, or clinical services in the field of maternal-fetal nutrition. Save to Dashboard Saved Pages Recognizing distinguished achievement in research, education, or clinical services in the field of maternal-fetal nutrition. The Agnes Higgins Award offers one recipient a cash award not tied to any research aims. A pioneer in devising methods of nutritional assessment and counseling, Mrs. Higgins greatly advanced the understanding of healthy eating and nutrition as a crucial factor in healthy pregnancy and prevention of low birth weight. While science, technology, and discovery in the maternal health field has progressed and researchers have begun asking ever more nuanced questions, nutrition remains at the forefront of a healthy pregnancy, with an increasing body of data pointing to its interconnectedness to maternal morbidity and mortality, as well as fetal and neonatal health. Award: A cash prize, a commemorative award reflecting the honor, and a presentation at the Pediatric Academic Society annual meeting Areas of research: Maternal-fetal nutrition Open to: Those candidates widely involved in maternal-fetal nutrition through teaching, research and/or clinical practice for at least five years Note: The current cycle is closed Nomination window opens: April 20, 2026 Nomination window closes: September 16, 2026 Selection Committee meets: Planned mid to late October 2026 Awardee is announced: December 2026 Eligibility To apply for the Agnes Higgins Award, candidates must have been widely involved in maternal-fetal nutrition through teaching, research, and/or clinical practice for at least five years; shown a demonstrable effect in raising the quality of maternal-fetal nutritional care through scholarly pursuits, research, education, and/or practice; and demonstrated an ability to apply maternal-fetal nutritional standards of practice and/or facilitate their implementation by others. How to nominate Nominations are accepted from those in the field as well as previous Agnes Higgins awardees. Self-nominations are accepted. If you would like a nomination package and more details, please contact Courtney Dower or Jonathan Cherry at [email protected] . How to nominate: Download a nomination form here and a copy of the Call for Nominations, including instructions here , or request a nomination form and call for nominations document by email from Courtney Dower or Jonathan Cherry at [email protected] and then submit it with all required attachments back to [email protected] by September 16, 2026. Required attachments include: A written description of the nominee’s achievements in maternal-fetal nutrition (300 word maximum) A list of nominee’s publications most relevant to the achievement for which the nomination is made The nominee’s curriculum vitae Letters from colleagues in support of the nominee’s qualifications and achievements (maximum of seven) Manuscript samples (maximum of three) Awardee partnership expectations March of Dimes works with a variety of researchers from around the world. Our hope is that our awardees view their time as scholars, grantees, or center partners as mutually beneficial, and with value beyond the monetary consideration. We expect our awardees to attend key meetings that pertain to their award program, or assign an appropriate delegate if not possible. We expect members of our research centers to collaborate scientifically and collegially with other centers or nonprofit organizations that are identified during the course of the award period. We expect that our awardees will attend scientific meetings that may be established by March of Dimes and use good faith efforts to help March of Dimes raise funds for future awards through attendance at some events, interviews, or other public-facing opportunities. These efforts are intended to amplify success of our current and future awardees. Questions: Please direct any questions to [email protected] . 2024 award recipient Jose Villar, MD, MPH, MSc, FRCOG Dr. Villar has spent more than a half-century researching the effect of maternal nutrition on the health, growth, and development of babies. 2022-23 award recipient Erica P. Gunderson, PhD, MS, MPH Dr. Gunderson is the scientist behind decades-long studies that have produced some of the field’s most important and astounding findings on pregnancy and breastfeeding’s links to diabetes and cardiovascular disease in young women. 2021 award recipient Nancy Krebs, MD, MS Dr. Krebs serves as the Head of the Division of Nutrition and Associate Vice Chair of Academic Affairs in the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Colorado School of Medicine. Johnston, Jr., MD Prize The March of Dimes Richard B. Johnston, Jr., MD Prize recognizes an outstanding scientist who has profoundly advanced the science around prenatal development, pregnancy, and birth. Save to Dashboard Saved Pages Celebrating scientists who have dedicated their lives to translational research The March of Dimes Richard B. Johnston, Jr., MD Prize honors outstanding scientists who profoundly advance the science that underlies our understanding of pregnancy, parturition, and prenatal development. Created as a tribute to Dr. Jonas Salk shortly before his death in 1995, the Prize has been awarded annually since 1996. It’s now named in recognition of Dr. Johnston, March of Dimes Medical Director when the Prize was initiated. He is a member of the National Academy of Medicine. To date, eight recipients have gone on to win Nobel Prizes. View list of previous recipients . The Prize carries a cash award and a physical commemorative award presented to the awardee at the Society for Reproductive Investigation (SRI) Annual Meeting where the awardee will also give a lecture. Award details: Cash prize, commemorative award, and a President’s Talk at the Society for Reproductive Investigation Annual Meeting Areas of research: Prenatal development and pregnancy and parturition Open to: Nominees are scientific leaders who have pioneered research to advance our understanding of prenatal development and pregnancy and parturition. March of Dimes looks for candidates whose work involves translational and impactful scientific discoveries that may lead to interventions or preventions that improve the health of moms and babies. Note: The current cycle is closed Nomination window opens: May 11, 2026 Nomination window closes: October 2, 2026 Selection Committee meets: Planned mid to late October 2026 Awardee is announced: November 2026 How to nominate: Nominators should submit the information listed in the how to nominate section below via email attachment to Courtney Dower or Jonathan Cherry at [email protected] ) by October 2, 2026. Eligibility Nominations are welcome for late career, outstanding scientists who have profoundly advanced the science around prenatal development, pregnancy, and birth, and who do not hold current or active March of Dimes grants or contracts. How to nominate Nominations may come from any scientists in the field who can provide a compelling nomination package for scientific leaders who have pioneered research to advance our understanding of prenatal development and pregnancy. No self-nominations are accepted. Nominators should submit the below information via email attachment to [email protected] by October 2, 2026. The nomination must include the following information in this order: Nominator's information Name Professional title and affiliation Address Telephone number Email address Signature Candidate's personal information Name Professional title and affiliation Address Telephone number Email address Candidate's nomination form Curriculum vitae A narrative biographic sketch (250 words) Statement of the nomination describing the impact of work in our understanding of prenatal development and pregnancy (150 words) Summary of scientific contributions on which nomination is based Nominees must be available to give a lecture during the 2027 Society for Reproductive Investigation Annual meeting on March 16-20, 2027 in Glasgow, United Kingdom.
